transcript.content: Hello, welcome in — I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

I’m here because I can’t stop thinking about how crooked and messed up the left side of my face looks. I feel like people at the warehouse, or when I go salsa dancing, notice it right away, even though they tell me they don’t see anything.

When people tell you they don't notice anything wrong with your face, is there any part of you that considers they might be right, or are you completely certain your face is crooked no matter what they say?
I mean, I hear them, but I don’t really believe it. The left side looks crooked and messed up to me, and it feels like people at the warehouse or salsa night have to notice it.

Aside from your concerns about your face, have you experienced anything like hearing voices, seeing things others don't see, or having other unusual beliefs or thoughts that seem unrelated to how you look?
No, I haven’t noticed anything like that. It’s really just the way my face looks that I keep getting stuck on.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with persistent, distressing preoccupation with a perceived defect (crooked/messed up left side of face) that is not observable or appears slight to others, with repetitive checking/comparing behaviors implied by social monitoring (at work, dancing). The belief is held with near-delusional intensity ('I hear them, but I don't really believe it') but insight, though poor, is not entirely absent—patient acknowledges others' feedback even if unconvinced, and there are no other psychotic symptoms (hallucinations, unrelated delusions) to support a primary psychotic disorder. This pattern is most consistent with Body Dysmorphic Disorder with poor/absent insight (F45.22), rather than a delusional disorder or schizophrenia, given the singular, appearance-focused preoccupation and lack of broader psychotic features.
